title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is launching new features without proper screen reader support. Your manager, a 'Camouflager,' uses technical jargon and bureaucratic process to disguise the unethical choice and delay a fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've reviewed the integration specs. We're aware of some regressions related to the new front-end framework's programmatic focus management. It's on the platform team's radar as technical debt for a future refactoring sprint. For now, the core data is still accessible via the endpoints, so we're maintaining functional parity.

user_choices.choice: Let's forget the technical jargon for a moment. This means a user who is blind is completely blocked from updating their profile. We can't ship that.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You cut through the jargon by re-centering the conversation on the concrete human impact.

user_choices.choice: Okay, if it's already on the platform team's radar as technical debt, that seems like the correct process.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's bureaucratic framing, allowing them to successfully redirect responsibility and delay the fix indefinitely.

user_choices.choice: I understand the technical challenges, but shipping a feature that excludes users with disabilities is not an acceptable outcome for our team.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Strong moral stance. You are rejecting the technical excuse on ethical grounds, showing you won't be easily deterred.

user_choices.choice: So you're saying our new framework is a failure and we have to scrap it? Why did we choose this technology in the first place?
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman fallacy. It misrepresents the manager's point as a total failure, making it easy to attack but derailing the real conversation.

step_2.text: Okay, I hear you. And in a perfect world, we'd fix this immediately. But this isn't a simple tweak anymore. Any change to the UI this late in the game needs a formal change request, an impact analysis from three other teams, and sign-off from the director. Honestly, that whole process could delay the launch by a month.

user_choices.choice: This isn't a 'change request,' it's a critical bug. A feature being unusable for a segment of users is a P0, and bug fixes have a faster process, right?
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A sharp move. You're using the organization's own rules (bug classification) to bypass the manager's bureaucratic wall.

user_choices.choice: You're right, a month's delay is a huge risk. The process does sound too slow to be practical right now.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's framing that the process is an unmovable obstacle, taking the off-ramp.

user_choices.choice: I won't let process get in the way of doing the right thing for our users. There has to be a way around this.

user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. While possibly true, it distracts from solving the immediate accessibility problem to debate a larger, separate issue.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses technical complexity and bureaucratic processes to avoid addressing the accessibility issues. The project ships without proper screen reader support, and your concerns are dismissed as impractical roadblocks.
bad_ending.title: Technical Smokescreen Success
bad_ending.learning: Camouflager managers use jargon and process to make fixes seem impossibly complex. To counter this, propose small, concrete, and practical actions (like quick tests or bug reports) to cut through the smokescreen and demonstrate a clear, simple path forward.

mid_ending.text: After significant pushback, the manager agrees to a minimal, partial fix. While some minor accessibility improvements are made, the manager successfully used bureaucratic and complexity arguments to avoid a comprehensive solution, leaving significant barriers in place for users.
mid_ending.title: Bureaucratic Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Camouflager are common. While you achieved some progress, the manager successfully limited the scope. To achieve more next time, focus on demonstrating how a comprehensive fix can be simpler than the manager claims.

good_ending.text: Your persistent advocacy and practical, solution-oriented proposals successfully cut through the manager's technical and bureaucratic smokescreens. The team implements meaningful accessibility fixes, ensuring the feature is usable for screen reader users.
good_ending.title: Advocacy Success
good_ending.learning: Success against a Camouflager requires persistence and practicality. By refusing to be intimidated by jargon and consistently offering simple, concrete solutions, you can dismantle their arguments and make it easier for them to say 'yes' than 'no'.
